title: Why Dating Costs So Much Now (Apps Charge You to Stay Single)
sources: Match Group FY2025 results / Business of Apps 'Match Statistics' (2026): Match Group (Tinder, Hinge, Match.com, etc.) reported ~$3.5 billion revenue in 2025

Business of Apps 'Bumble Statistics' (2026): Bumble reported ~$782 million revenue in 2025, a ~9.6% decline year-over-year; Business of Apps 'Dating App Market' (2026): the dating-app industry took in just over $6 billion in 2025

FTC v. Match Group (filed Sept 2019): FTC alleged Match.com used communications from accounts it had already flagged as likely fraudulent to send 'someone's interested in you' notices that pushed non-subscribers to pay; FTC press release (Aug 2025): Match Group agreed to pay $14 million and to change its advertising, guarantee, and cancellation practices to resolve the FTC's claims, without admitting wrongdoing

Industry data on paywalled features (SwipeStats/dating-app-economy roundups, 2026): common subscription-gated features include seeing who liked you, unlimited likes/swipes, undoing swipes ('rewind'), and boosted visibility; roughly 7% of dating-app users worldwide pay for premium features (about 35% of U.S. users have paid at some point)

Variable-reward / behavioral-design concept (widely documented in behavioral psychology and tech-design research, e.g. B.F. Skinner's variable-ratio reinforcement, cited in analyses of swipe-based app design): unpredictable rewards (occasional matches) drive repeated-checking behavior similar to slot machines

BMO Real Financial Progress Index / Ipsos survey of 2,501 U.S. adults, Dec 29, 2025-Jan 27, 2026 (published Feb 11, 2026): average 'all-in' cost of a date (including prep and gas) reached $189, up 12.5% from $168 the year before ('date-flation'); average American adult spends about $2,323/year on dates; ~47% of single adults said dating no longer feels financially worth it; average number of dates fell to ~12/year from ~14

beats.text: Dave checks his banking app. Forty dollars, gone again, to a dating app subscription.
He opens the app. Zero new matches. Same as last month. Same as the month before that.
And here's the twist. The app is not broken. It's working exactly as designed.
Because a match isn't really the goal. Dave, still paying, still swiping, that's the goal.
The longer he stays single and subscribed, the more the app makes.
Today: how dating apps actually make money, the myth about the algorithm, and how to date without going broke.

beats.chapter: The Dating Economy Is Bigger Than You Think
beats.text: Let's start with the size of this thing. Dave thinks he's using a free app.
Match Group alone, the company behind Tinder, Hinge, and Match dot com, made about three and a half billion dollars in twenty twenty five.
Bumble made about seven hundred eighty two million. And that was actually a drop from the year before.
Across the whole industry, dating apps pulled in just over six billion dollars last year. From people looking for love, or at least a Friday night plan.
Tinder alone made about one point nine billion of that, even after paying subscribers fell for eight quarters straight. Fewer people paying, but more money out of each one who does.
Dave got frustrated with Tinder, so he deleted it and tried Hinge instead. Same result.
Here's the twist. Tinder, Hinge, Match dot com, Ok Cupid, Plenty of Fish, and several more, are all owned by the very same company.
So when Dave 'switches apps' to escape one subscription, he's very often still paying the exact same parent company.
It's less like choosing between competing stores, and more like walking to a different aisle inside the same supermarket.
Here's the part that stings a little. A happy couple who deletes the app is a lost customer.
If Dave meets someone on day two and cancels his subscription, the app makes almost nothing off him.
If Dave stays single, keeps swiping, and keeps paying every month, the app makes far more, month after month.
That doesn't mean the apps want everyone miserable forever. It means the business math rewards you staying a customer, not you finding 'the one' on day one.

beats.chapter: Myth-Bust: The Algorithm Wants You to Match
beats.text: Most people think the app's algorithm is working hard to find their soulmate. Nope.
The algorithm is trained to keep you using the app. Matching you instantly, every time, would actually work against that.
In twenty nineteen, the F T C sued Match Group. The claim: the company used flagged, likely fraudulent accounts to send 'someone likes you' emails, to push people into paying.
In twenty twenty five, Match Group agreed to pay fourteen million dollars, and to change its ads, guarantees, and cancellation process, to settle those claims.
The company didn't admit wrongdoing. But the lesson stands. The notification that pulls you back into the app is a business tool, not a promise.
So what does Dave's forty dollars a month actually buy?
Seeing who already liked him. Unlimited swipes, instead of a daily limit. Undoing an accidental left swipe. Being shown higher up in other people's stacks.
None of these features find him a better person. They remove a small annoyance the app put there in the first place.
It's a lot like our credit card video's raccoon. First it builds a tiny toll booth in your way. Then it charges you to skip the line.
Only about seven percent of dating app users worldwide actually pay for any of it. The other ninety three percent are the free product, shown ads and constant upgrade offers.
Ever wonder why swiping feels a little like a slot machine?
Because the reward is random. Most swipes get nothing. Every so often, one gets a match. Your brain loves that pattern.
Psychologists call it a variable reward. It's the same trick that makes slot machines, and social media feeds, so hard to put down.
The app isn't lying to you about your matches. It's just built on a shape that keeps you opening it, once, twice, twenty times a day.
And it's not just the app. Actually going on the date costs more now too.
A twenty twenty six survey put the average American date night, including getting ready and gas money, at about one hundred eighty nine dollars.
That's up about twelve and a half percent in a single year. Regular inflation didn't move anywhere near that fast.
Add it up over a year, and the average adult spends around two thousand three hundred twenty three dollars, just on date nights.
No wonder almost half of single adults in that survey said dating just doesn't feel financially worth it anymore. Many said they now go on fewer dates, or pick cheaper ones on purpose.

beats.chapter: How Much This Generation Actually Spends
beats.text: So how much does dating itself cost, app plus dates, every month?
People who date actively, not just casually, spend over three hundred dollars a month on the whole thing, apps and dates combined.
But a lot of Gen Z has opted out of the spending, not the dating. In one survey, fifty three percent of Gen Z adults said they spend zero dollars a month on dating.
About a third spend under a hundred dollars. So this generation isn't cheap, or lazy. Plenty of them have just noticed the math, and would rather save the money.
So who wins here, while Dave keeps swiping alone?
The dating apps win, every single month Dave stays subscribed and single. That's recurring revenue, built from a habit, not a purchase.
Restaurants and bars win too, from date-flation, higher prices on the exact things people do on a first date.
Dave only wins if he treats the app like a tool to meet someone, not a slot machine to check between meetings.
None of this means dating apps are evil, or that nobody finds real love on them. Plenty of people do. It just means the business quietly profits either way.

beats.chapter: How to Date Without Going Broke
beats.text: So how do you play this smarter? Remember, this is education, not relationship advice.
One. Try the free tier first, seriously. Most matches happen without paying a single cent.
Two. Set a real budget for dates, the same way you'd budget for groceries. It stops 'date-flation' from becoming a surprise.
Three. Move to an actual phone call or a meetup faster. The app's job is done the moment you swap numbers. Don't let it linger.
Four. If a month goes by with a paid subscription and zero real conversations, that's a signal to cancel, not to upgrade.
Five. Cheap dates work fine. A coffee, or a walk, tells you more about a person than a fancy dinner ever will.
None of that costs forty dollars a month. Most of it costs nothing at all.
So let's recap.
One. Dating apps made over six billion dollars last year, and a match that ends your subscription is actually bad for their business.
Two. The algorithm isn't rooting for you. It's built to keep you swiping, and actual dates got a lot more expensive too.
Three. The free tier, a real budget, and moving off the app fast beat almost every paid feature.
Next time, Dave finally gets the raise he's been asking for. So why does his paycheck look exactly the same?
Subscribe, so Dave can keep explaining money. It's free. Which, this episode taught us, is rarer than it sounds.
